images.title: One number for a group?
images.purpose: Show that heights in a group vary from person to person, raising the question of whether one number can stand for the whole group.
images.composition: A single row of seven flat figures of different heights across the middle of the frame, with one dashed level line across them and white space above and below.
exact_structure: Exactly 7 flat, faceless child figures standing in a row on one grey (#6B7280) ground line, evenly spaced, all in teal (#0072B2).
Their heights, from left to right, in relative units: 128, 140, 134, 145, 131, 139, 137, so no two figures are the same height; the 4th figure is the tallest and the 1st is the shortest.
One reddish purple (#CC79A7) dashed horizontal line crosses the row at the height 136, above some heads and below others.
At the right end of the dashed line, a reddish purple question mark.
One short caption centred under the ground line reading: Heights vary. Can one number stand for all?
labels: Heights vary. Can one number stand for all?
rejection: any two figures of equal height
the dashed line drawn above every head or below every head
height numbers written on the figures
images.takeaway: Heights differ, so describing a group needs a number that represents everyone fairly.
images.description: Seven teal figures of different heights stand in a row, crossed by one purple dashed line with a question mark.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video for this concept.
images.teaching_notes: Ask whether any single figure's height could fairly describe the whole row, and keep the question for the next topics.

image_decisions.why: A row of unequal heights makes the framing question visible at a glance.
